ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
The following information applies for the next two problems. A circuit has a power source of $\mathcal{E}=5.82 \mathrm{~V}$ connected to three elements in series: an inductor with $L=12.5 \mathrm{mH}$, a capacitor with $C=48.5 \mu \mathrm{F}$, and a diode with threshold voltage $V_{0}=0.65 \mathrm{~V}$. (Of course, the polarity of the diode is aligned with that of the power source.) You close the switch, and after some time, the voltage across the capacitor becomes constant. (Note: An ideal diode with threshold voltage $V_{0}$ is one whose IV characteristic is given by $I=0$ for $V<V_{0}$ and $V=V_{0}$ for $I>0$.)

<image_1>

How much time (in seconds) has elapsed before the voltage across the capacitor becomes constant?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a single series circuit; at the bottom there are a power supply and a switch, and at the top there are, in sequence, an inductor L, a capacitor C, and a diode; the diode direction is matched with the power supply polarity, so that after the switch is closed, in the initial current direction, the diode is forward conducting. Reasoning: During the period when the diode is conducting, the diode voltage drop is fixed at V0 = 0.65 V. Let the capacitor charge be q, the current I = dq/dt, with initial q(0)=0 and I(0)=0. Write KVL for the series circuit: L dI/dt + q/C + V0 = E, therefore L q'' + q/C = E - V0. The solution of this equation is q = C(E - V0)(1 - cos(ωt)), where ω = 1/sqrt(LC), and the current I = C(E - V0)ω sin(ωt). The capacitor voltage becomes constant when the current first returns to zero; after this, if the current attempts to reverse direction, the diode cuts off, so charging stops. The first I=0 with t>0 corresponds to ωt = π, therefore t = π sqrt(LC). Substituting L = 12.5e-3 H, C = 48.5e-6 F: t = π sqrt((12.5e-3)(48.5e-6)) = 2.446e-3 s.

method.method_draft: Use a direct time-domain differential-equation solution. From the diagram, identify a single series loop containing the battery, switch, inductor, capacitor, and forward-oriented diode. From the text, take \(\mathcal E=5.82\,\mathrm V\), \(V_0=0.65\,\mathrm V\), \(L=12.5\,\mathrm{mH}\), and \(C=48.5\,\mu\mathrm F\). While the diode conducts, it has fixed drop \(V_0\), so KVL gives \(L\,dI/dt+q/C+V_0=\mathcal E\), with \(I=dq/dt\), \(q(0)=0\), and \(I(0)=0\). Solve \(Lq''+q/C=\mathcal E-V_0\), giving \(q=C(\mathcal E-V_0)(1-\cos\omega t)\), \(I=C(\mathcal E-V_0)\omega\sin\omega t\), where \(\omega=1/\sqrt{LC}\). The capacitor voltage becomes constant when the current first returns to zero and the diode blocks further reverse current, at \(\omega t=\pi\). Thus \(t=\pi\sqrt{LC}=\pi\sqrt{(12.5\times10^{-3})(48.5\times10^{-6})}\approx2.446\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm s\).

method.method_draft: Use the LC step-response/phase-space turning-point argument. From the image, treat the closed circuit as an undamped series LC branch driven by a constant effective voltage source as long as the diode is on. From the text, the diode is ideal with fixed forward drop \(V_0\), so during forward conduction the LC pair sees a constant drive \(\mathcal E-V_0\). An undamped LC circuit driven from rest by a DC step has capacitor voltage \(V_C(t)=(\mathcal E-V_0)(1-\cos(t/\sqrt{LC}))\): it starts at zero with zero current, reaches its first opposite phase-space turning point after half a natural period, and at that point the inductor current is zero. Since after that instant the natural LC motion would require current reversal, the diode becomes reverse/nonconducting and isolates the capacitor, freezing its voltage. Therefore the required time is half the LC period, \(T/2=\pi\sqrt{LC}\). Substituting \(L=12.5\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm H\) and \(C=48.5\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm F\) gives \(t\approx2.446\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm s\).

The solution of this equation is q = C(E - V0)(1 - cos(ωt)), where ω = 1/sqrt(LC), and the current I = C(E - V0)ω sin(ωt). The capacitor voltage becomes constant when the current first returns to zero; after this, if the current attempts to reverse direction, the diode cuts off, so charging stops. The first I=0 with t>0 corresponds to ωt = π, therefore t = π sqrt(LC). Substituting L = 12.5e-3 H, C = 48.5e-6 F: t = π sqrt((12.5e-3)(48.5e-6)) = 2.446e-3 s.
